A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v3 reports original evaluations of ten models on CRUXEval and SemTrace, including line-removal experiments, arithmetic sensitivity tests, and appendix analyses.

after.justification: v4 retains these original results and adds JavaScript and PHP evaluations with four existing models in Section 5.1 and Appendix D.

M1.justification: The counterfactual line-removal method and SemTrace generation procedure remain unchanged. JavaScript and PHP versions use the same procedure with language-appropriate syntax; no new algorithmic component or model modification is introduced.

E1.justification: The Python-only evaluation expands to JavaScript and PHP using CRUXEval-X subsets, matching CodeSearchNet distractors, and translated SemTrace tasks. This substantially broadens programming-language coverage for retrieval and output prediction.

E2.justification: The original model comparisons and Python-interpreter reference are retained. The added language experiments use existing participants: Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B, Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 3 27B, and Codestral 22B v0.1. No comparator is added or removed within the retained experiments.

E3.justification: The distractor counts, eleven target positions, greedy decoding, zero-shot evaluation, and accuracy measures remain unchanged; v4 explicitly applies the same protocol to the additional languages. Visual inspection confirms that v3 already plots negative relative accuracy changes, so v4's revised wording and delta labels clarify the existing measure.

E4.justification: v4 adds a substantial cross-language generalization test, selecting JavaScript and PHP for their reported low correlation with Python and testing whether the lexical-semantic dissociation persists. Figures 10–11 also expose language-specific failures. The existing line-removal, higher-digit, partial-match, and unresolved-output analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report exponential fits with bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals in Figures 1 and 3. No new repeated-run counts, seeds, significance tests, or uncertainty-reporting procedures are introduced.

E6.justification: v4 adds extensive language-specific results, reporting median relative accuracy drops of 34.72% and 14.35% on CRUXEval-JS/PHP versus 80.39% and 76.12% on SemTrace-JS/PHP. The Python values in Tables 1–2 and curves in Figures 1–9 are retained. Figure 11 explicitly identifies −100% for zero-baseline PHP cases as a visualization convention, not a measured relative drop.

T1.justification: The sensitivity definition in Equation 1 and the SemTrace guessing-probability calculation remain unchanged. The added statement that the sensitivity estimator depends on the model clarifies its interpretation without revising the formal mathematics.

C1.justification: The introduction's contributions now explicitly claim validation across Python, JavaScript, and PHP. The principal claims about lexical-semantic dissociation, counterfactual sensitivity measurement, and SemTrace remain unchanged in the abstract and conclusion.

C2.justification: Interpretive scope expands through the new Broader Implications section connecting semantic recall to legal and policy procedures. v4 also adds an argument against an out-of-distribution explanation, qualifies the estimator as model-dependent, interprets PHP failures as possible language-dependent shortcut reliance, and removes the obsolete Python-only limitation.

D1.justification: v4 adds a code-repository link, documents syntax adaptation and matching distractor sources for the additional languages, and corrects the Llama 3.1 license entry. The core prompt instructions, hardware, software versions, and reported execution costs are retained.

R1.justification: v4 adds Yang et al. (2025b) on mutated code-reasoning problems, Xu et al. (2025) on CRUXEval-X, and Jurayj et al. (2026) on tax reasoning. These extend the supporting literature without replacing the existing related-work framing or central novelty claims.

P1.justification: v4 makes localized wording and terminology corrections, fixes a figure cross-reference and the unfinished Table 2 caption, and adds acknowledgments. It inserts Broader Implications and the language appendix while retaining most of the original exposition and section organization.

P2.justification: v4 adds two substantial multi-panel figures for JavaScript and PHP and restyles existing plots with explicit delta labels and differentiated line styles. Licensing tables relocate, captions are revised, and the retained prompt figures are renumbered from 10–12 to 12–14.

improvement.justification: The added language experiments address v3's explicit Python-only limitation and strengthen evidence for generalization. The code link, estimator qualification, and clearer plotting labels also improve usability and transparency. These gains are bounded: zero-baseline SemTrace-PHP cases cannot establish relative positional degradation, as Figure 11 acknowledges. The core Python evidence remains unchanged.
